You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
The failing test case `testEqualsCS1` checks the behavior of `StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence)` with `StringBuilder` inputs of different lengths. Specifically, it expects `false` when the two sequences have differing lengths.

The current bug report summary says: `c0.m0(CharSequence cs1, CharSequence cs2) can fail with String Index OBE`, implying an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (String Index Out of Bounds Exception) occurs when the two sequences have different lengths.

Inspection of `StringUtils.equals` shows that when both inputs are non-null and not both Strings, it defers to:
```java
CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches(cs1, false, 0, cs2, 0, Math.max(cs1.length(), cs2.length()));
```
Here, `length` for the `regionMatches` call is taken as the larger length of the two inputs (maximum length). This is suspicious because the `regionMatches` implementation iterates over the requested length, accessing each character at positions from start index up to length.

In `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches`, the code performs this loop:
```java
while (tmpLen-- > 0) {
    final char c1 = cs.charAt(index1++);
    final char c2 = substring.charAt(index2++);
    ...
}
```
The indices `index1` and `index2` are incremented from their starting points. If `length` exceeds the length of either `cs` or `substring`, then `charAt(index)` will throw an IndexOutOfBoundsException (which matches the report's String Index Out Of Bounds Exception).

Therefore, the bug is that `StringUtils.equals` uses the maximum length of the two CharSequences as the match region length, leading to out-of-bounds access if the sequences differ in length.

The fix should be to use the minimum length instead of maximum to avoid indexing beyond the short sequence's length. Also, since two sequences of different lengths cannot be equal, the method should immediately return false if their lengths differ instead of trying to compare a region beyond the shorter length.

The recent bug reports are unrelated to indexing or regionMatches, so they do not impact the diagnosis here.

This analysis explains why test lines 225 and 226 correctly get `false` (due to null checks), line 227 returns true (equal length and contents), but line 228 throws an exception because it compares sequences of different lengths using a too-large length parameter inside regionMatches.

This confirms that the root cause is the incorrect usage of `Math.max(cs1.length(), cs2.length())` as the length argument to `regionMatches` in `StringUtils.equals`.

The appropriate correction is to first check for length equality, and if not equal, return false; otherwise use the length (either length of cs1 or cs2) for regionMatches.

# Final recommendation:
Change `StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence)` to return false immediately if lengths differ before calling `regionMatches` with exact length equal to the length of either sequence.
Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
The failing test case `testEqualsCS1` expects that when comparing two `CharSequence` instances of different lengths, `StringUtils.equals` returns false. However, the current implementation calls `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches` with the length parameter as `Math.max(cs1.length(), cs2.length())`. This causes `regionMatches` to access indices beyond the length of the shorter sequence, leading to a String Index Out Of Bounds Exception (as described in the bug report). The root cause is that `StringUtils.equals` uses the maximum length instead of the minimum length or first checks length equality. To fix this, `StringUtils.equals` should return false immediately if lengths differ and only call `regionMatches` with the common length if they are equal.


Suggested method(s) to fix:
org.apache.commons.codec.binary.StringUtils.equals(java.lang.CharSequence,java.lang.CharSequence)

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
